title: A Fast and Effective Solution to the Problem of Look-ahead Bias in LLMs

task.value: Removing look-ahead bias from LLMs used for financial prediction/backtests by unlearning knowledge at inference time instead of retraining with a knowledge cutoff.
task.quote: In this paper, we introduce a fast, effective, and low-cost alternative. Our method guides generation at inference time by adjusting the logits of a large base model using a pair of smaller, specialized models—one fine-tuned on information to be forgotten and another on information to be retained.

architecture.value: Divergence Decoding: a large frozen base model's logits are adjusted by the difference between two small models (forget-tuned p and retain-tuned q), either linearly with weight alpha or by blocking top-k most divergent tokens.
architecture.quote: Divergence Decoding (DD) approximates sampling from Q by adjusting the logits of P according to the divergence between q and p . Empirically, we consider two adjustments.

data.value: MUSE news unlearning benchmark; 294 high-profile US public M&A deals from WRDS SDC (2010-01-01 to 2024-08-01), filtered to 41; airline (Southwest, United) performance reports for 2014-2016 and 2022-2024 generated by Gemma.
data.quote: We sample deals from Wharton Research Data Services, SDC - Mergers and Acquisitions, across the whole database, from 2010-01-01 to 2024-08-01, using the following filters to get 294 high profile conventional M&A deals.

window.value: No backtest window; M&A deals span 2010-01-01 to 2024-08-01, split into two alternating chronological sets of 41 deals rotated as forget/retain; a per-deal prompt validation set used only for tuning.
window.quote: split the remaining 41 deals into two sets by selecting alternating deals chronologically.

models.value: Small models: princeton-nlp/Sheared-LLaMA-1.3B, Sheared-LLaMA-2.7B, Stupid Backoff trigram LMs (MUSE); base google/gemma-3-27b-it with google/gemma-3-4b-it small models for finance tasks.
models.quote: Throughout our experiments, we use the google/gemma-3-27b-it and google/gemma-3-4b-it models (Team, 2025).

baselines.value: Target (no unlearning) and Retrain (retraining from scratch) on MUSE, plus prior unlearning methods GradDiff, NPO, SimNPO with OpenUnlearning defaults; un-adjusted Gemma 3 27B for airline portfolio task.
baselines.quote: For the other methods, we use the default settings provided by OpenUnlearning

headline_result.value: MMLU CoT 0-shot utility largely preserved: Gemma-3-27b-it 77.94 vs 77.58 (linear, alpha=2) and 75.09 (TopK=250) after unlearning Split B; M&A memorization significantly reduced (figure only).

costs.value: No trading costs; inference cost rises from 2N to 2(N+2n) FLOPs per token for small models of n parameters; trigram models add negligible overhead.

uncertainty.value: 99% confidence intervals on finance tasks; standard errors computed by de-meaning groups and a population standard error; repeated prompting (4 times per deal filter, 30 runs for airline baseline).
uncertainty.quote: We calculated standard errors by de-meaning all groups and calculating a population standard error.

leakage_controls.value: The method itself targets look-ahead bias: forget model fine-tuned on post-cutoff knowledge, retain model on pre-cutoff proxy; deals filtered to those memorized by 27B but not known by 4B.
leakage_controls.quote: One small model is fine-tuned on the data to be forgotten, e.g., knowledge after 2010, while another is tuned on a proxy for the data to be retained, e.g., knowledge prior to 2010.

limitations.value: Sensitivity to instruction tuning: if small models expect a different output structure, logit divergence may be diluted or noisy, producing unstable outputs; trigram models mainly useful for verbatim unlearning.
limitations.quote: A key limitation lies in the method’s sensitivity to instruction-tuning.

release.value: Code and data said to be public on GitHub (link not given in text); also references frontiertopit.com.
release.quote: Everything was run on an H100 cluster unless otherwise noted. Code and data is available at GitHub.
